module_title: Criteria for Protection, Infringement vs Passing Off, and Fair Dealing
introduction: This intermediate tier explores the strict legal criteria an invention or mark must meet to get protection. It dissects the difference between Trademark Infringement and Passing Off, and the statutory defense of Fair Dealing in Copyright.

core_concepts.title: Criteria for Patentability
core_concepts.description:
To get a patent, an invention MUST satisfy the 'NUN' test:
1. Novelty: It must be totally new. It cannot be published or known to the public anywhere in the world before the filing date.
2. Utility (Industrial Application): It must be capable of being made or used in an industry.
3. Non-obviousness (Inventive Step): It must involve a technical advance that is NOT obvious to a person skilled in that specific field.

core_concepts.title: Trademarks: Infringement vs. Passing Off
core_concepts.description:
A highly tested commercial law concept.
- Infringement: A statutory remedy available ONLY to **Registered Trademarks**. If someone uses an identical/deceptively similar mark to your registered mark, you sue for infringement.
- Passing Off: A common law (tort) remedy available to **Unregistered Trademarks**. If your brand isn't registered, but you have built immense goodwill, and someone tries to sell their goods by pretending they are yours (riding on your goodwill), you sue for passing off. You must prove Goodwill, Misrepresentation, and Damage.

core_concepts.title: Non-Conventional Trademarks
core_concepts.description:
Modern trademark law protects more than just words and logos. If they are 'graphically representable' and 'distinctive', you can register:
- Sound Marks: The Yahoo yodel, the MGM lion roar, the ICICI Bank jingle.
- Shape Marks: The distinct shape of the Coca-Cola bottle or Toblerone bottle.
- Color Marks: Difficult to get, but a specific combination of colors exclusively associated with a brand can be registered.

core_concepts.title: Copyright: The Doctrine of Fair Dealing (Section 52)
core_concepts.description:
Copyright is not absolute. The law allows the public to use copyrighted material without permission for specific purposes, known as 'Fair Dealing'.
- Valid Fair Dealing: Using small excerpts for private research, criticism/review, reporting current events, or educational use by a teacher in a classroom.
- Note: 'Fair Use' is the American doctrine (which is broader); India uses the stricter, specifically listed 'Fair Dealing' under Section 52.

important_entities.name: Well-Known Trademark
important_entities.key_fact: Protection across all classes of goods.
important_entities.significance: Normally, TM protection is limited to your specific class of goods (e.g., a shoe brand TM doesn't stop someone from using the same name for a software company). BUT, if a mark is declared 'Well-Known' (like Google, Tata, Rolex), it gets cross-class protection. You cannot open a 'Rolex Bakery' or 'Google Cements'.

trap_alerts_and_exceptions.explanation: If A (a software developer) writes code for B (an IT company) during the course of his regular employment, who owns the copyright? **The Employer (B)**. The general rule is the author is the first owner, BUT an exception exists for 'contract of service' (employment). Under Section 17, the employer automatically becomes the first owner of the copyright unless agreed otherwise.

mnemonics_and_tricks.explanation: Use the NUN acronym to remember the three absolute prerequisites for granting a patent.

exam_strategy_tips: If a UPSC or Judiciary question asks 'Which legal remedy is available to protect the goodwill of an unregistered trademark?', select **Passing Off**.
